short_summary: Dr. Andrew Huberman explains the biological mechanisms regulating hair growth and hair loss, detailing how follicle stem cell niches, microcirculation, and dihydrotestosterone (DHT) determine hair retention. He evaluates the efficacy and safety profiles of both mechanical interventions, like microneedling, and biochemical treatments, including minoxidil, finasteride, dutasteride, and ketoconazole.
long_summary: Hair follicles operate through a continuous cycle comprising three primary phases: anagen (active growth lasting up to several years), catagen (follicular regression from the base up), and telogen (quiescence and shedding). Every hair relies on an endogenous stem cell niche within the dermal papilla and hair bulb, which requires a dense capillary network delivering oxygen and nutrients to maintain keratin synthesis. Hair loss, primarily androgenic alopecia, is predominantly mediated by the conversion of testosterone into dihydrotestosterone (DHT) via the enzyme 5-alpha reductase. Elevated local DHT binds to androgen receptors in genetically susceptible scalp zones, miniaturizing the follicle and significantly truncating the anagen phase. Therapeutic strategies divide into mechanical and biochemical approaches. Mechanical methods, specifically microneedling at depths of 1.0 to 2.5 mm, induce localized micro-inflammation that reactivates dormant stem cells and encourages follicular transition from the telogen back into the anagen phase. Blood flow-enhancing agents such as minoxidil or low-dose tadalafil prolong anagen duration via vasodilation, while topical caffeine acts as a phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibitor, elevating cyclic AMP and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) to protect follicles from apoptosis. To address the primary hormonal driver, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors like finasteride and dutasteride suppress DHT synthesis. Because finasteride exhibits a logarithmic dose-response curve, micro-doses provide significant DHT reduction while minimizing systemic side effects, such as post-finasteride syndrome or elevated prolactin. Mild adjuncts, such as 2% ketoconazole shampoo and saw palmetto, provide supplemental support by altering sebum biochemistry and offering mild local anti-androgenic effects. Meta-analyses demonstrate that multimodal regimens combining mechanical disruption (microneedling) with chemical DHT inhibition yield the highest rates of follicular recovery and hair regrowth.

Incorporate 2% ketoconazole shampoo: Using a 2% ketoconazole shampoo 2–4 times weekly with 3–5 minutes of scalp contact time reduces local scalp inflammation, modulates fungal activity, and offers mild local anti-androgenic benefits.
